entries.title: He Who Was, Is and Will Be
entries.subtitle: Before the Ages · The Creator

paragraphs.text: He Who Was, Is and Will Be is the supreme Creator, the God of all gods and of the universe. He is known by that title alone. He stands beyond the Holy Seven, beyond the Old Gods and the New Gods, and beyond every other being in the order of being.

sources.note: 01 - Cosmology/He Who Was, Is and Will Be.md
sources.section: He Who Was, Is and Will Be

paragraphs.text: No chronicle tells of any rival or peer to Him, of any shape in which He has shown Himself, or of any priesthood or worship kept in His name. He is too remote to take any part in the wars and crowns of Aoaz. How He made the Seven, and how He made all that exists, no chronicle tells.

sources.note: 01 - Cosmology/He Who Was, Is and Will Be.md
sources.section: He Who Was, Is and Will Be

paragraphs.text: Below He Who Was, Is and Will Be, and above every ordinary order of being, stand the Holy Seven. They are the seven overwhelmingly powerful creators of the cosmos, and they made both the Old Gods and the New Gods.

The Seven are too vast and too far removed to take any part in the daily history of Aoaz. Most people of Aoaz do not believe that they ever existed. Ordinary folk know the Old Gods and the New Gods, but the Seven survive only as faint traces in the most distant myths.

The oldest writings call them the Seven Before Names, as if they came before naming, speech and history. Among sceptics they are the Seven Who Never Were, a dismissal of the oldest tales of creation. Later scholars mostly treat such manuscripts as fable.

Their own names, the powers each of them held, how often they acted and in what shape, no chronicle tells. Nor is it known whether He Who Was, Is and Will Be made them directly, or how such a making came to pass.

plate.subject: five empty stone thrones receding into mist

paragraphs.text: The scholars of Parim and Selen set out the order of being in two levels. Far above all stand He Who Was, Is and Will Be, the supreme Creator, and below Him the Holy Seven, the makers of the gods, all but absent from history. Beneath them lie the five ordinary orders, the beings the folk of Aoaz may meet.

First are the Gods, immortal, two generations within one order: the Old Gods and the New Gods. Next come the Great Spirits, the first rank of spirits, among them Volgan. Then come the Lesser Spirits, some strong enough to be taken for gods. Fourth are the Great Folk, elves, angels, demons and other immortals who are not spirits. Last are the Common Folk, men, dwarves and other mortal beings.

Only the Common Folk are mortal. Yet immortal does not mean unkillable. Golbran does not age, and still he can die; devils are bound to their bodies and can be slain. Whether immortal means only that a being does not age, in every order, is not known. Nor do the scholars agree to which order, if any, the ghosts, revenants and roaming dead belong.

The order records the kind of a being, not who wins when two of them meet. The Old Gods hold more fundamental power than the New Gods, yet the Fading binds them. Volgan, a Great Spirit, wields enormous power over realms and armies, and he once overcame a New God, though he is of a lower order. Rank is no measure of victory.

sources.section: Power is not the same as practical control

paragraphs.text: It is not known how many Old Gods and New Gods exist beyond Aoaz, how many lesser New Gods there are or what they are called, or how the immortal Great Folk first came into being.

plate.subject: colossal faceless ruins half sunk in a grey sea

paragraphs.text: The Old Gods are the first generation of gods, almost unimaginably ancient. The Holy Seven made them before the New Gods, and in the beginning they held far more power than the New Gods.

Across immense spans of time their strength, and their ability to wield it, have faded. This is called the Fading. The Old Gods are generally unable to take an active bodily form, and they rarely touch the world openly. Even so, an Old God in decline remains enormously powerful.

Zol, the God of Death, is an Old God and the only Old God in Aoaz. That does not prove that no Old Gods exist elsewhere, beyond Aoaz. Zol is also the exception to any simple tale of decline: his power grows slowly, every day, though the magic of Aoaz makes it hard for him to channel that power or take shape.

sources.section: Important qualification: Zol's power is growing

paragraphs.text: The Old Gods are known to the people of Aoaz from myth and old religion, though most think of them as lost or idle. The tales do not agree. One faith holds that the Old Gods are dead, another that they sleep, a third that they are hostile, and others say that they went away or hid themselves. What causes the Fading, no chronicle tells.
paragraphs.note: The three faiths that hold the Old Gods dead, sleeping or hostile are proposed.

plate.subject: a temple of many empty niches lit by lamps

paragraphs.text: The New Gods are a later generation of gods, made by the Holy Seven. They are younger than the Old Gods and less powerful at root, but widely known throughout Aoaz, and many are worshipped openly. Twelve main New Gods answer the twelve needs of mortals, and each of the twelve months honours one of them.
paragraphs.note: That many New Gods are worshipped openly is proposed.

paragraphs.text: In the order of the year the first six are Glernaen, of strength and counsel; Sulethe, of healing; Lumae, of shelter and the hearth; Maelwen, of fair weather and safe waters; Vaelei, of kin and birth; and Rasthel, of safe roads and fair exchange.

After them come Kerun, of protection; Aurlan, of daily bread; Ailtal, of justice and kept promises; Irumas, of skill and work; Gaelor, of a good death and remembrance; and Naisa, of hope and fortune. Glernaen, the God of Power and Wisdom, is the mightiest of the twelve.

The gods are never shown in the shape of men. Temple art shows them as presences of the heavens: light, stars, celestial forms and their signs made of the sky. No halo, no saintly face and no human body stands for a god.
Beside the twelve stand the lesser New Gods, whom no month honours, yet they are stronger than most Great Spirits. Their number and names are not known.
The Deliverer, whom Aoaz hailed as a New God for saving the world from Elzon at the end of the Third Age, is not one of the twelve. His worshippers keep a feast in his honour, not a month.

sources.section: Afrit in Third and Fourth Age religion

paragraphs.text: The Deliverer was Afrit. His worship was real, and so were his powers. Whether he ever belonged to the order of New Gods that the Holy Seven made is not known, and the faith of his priests proves nothing either way.

sources.section: Afrit in Third and Fourth Age religion

plate.subject: stars dimming over a dark horizon

paragraphs.text: The Fading is the power that binds the ancient Old Gods. Across extremely long ages their ability to wield their power, and to keep an active bodily form, has dwindled, though they still hold vast power within them.

The Fading is one reason why Zol cannot simply take a body, conquer Aoaz or use his enormous power freely. The other is the unusual magic of Aoaz itself, which resists his kind of divine power or fails to support it.

The Fading does not mean that Zol grows weaker. He gains power every day, very slowly, and still the Fading holds him. How much power he has, and how much of it he can show or direct in Aoaz, are separate matters.

sources.section: Important qualification: Zol's power is growing

paragraphs.text: No chronicle says that such a lapse would destroy him throughout the cosmos.

sources.section: Important qualification: Zol's power is growing

paragraphs.text: What causes the Fading, no chronicle tells. Some scholars tie it to the great age of the Old Gods, some to the history of the cosmos or to a law beneath it, and some hold that the essence of the Old Gods has grown into the foundations of the world itself. The scholars do not agree whether any of these is true.
paragraphs.note: The theory that the essence of the Old Gods has grown into the foundations of the world is proposed.

plate.subject: threads of pale light rising from forest and stone

paragraphs.text: Aoaz holds a magic of its own, or a condition of magic, that Zol finds unusually hard to draw upon or to work through. Together with the Fading, it sharply limits how freely he can act, immensely powerful though he remains.

Magic runs in the folk of Aoaz as well. The earliest generations of men were naturally better at magic than later men, and some of them held powers like those of gods without being gods. Aen himself was born from magic and power.

sources.section: The Ainu and the First Men

paragraphs.text: Some powers draw strength from particular lands. Elzon’s necromancy was sustained by the magic of the Ember Lands, and he lost power when he stayed in Aenor. He could not fully conquer the Magical Lands, where Varner, a Lesser Spirit, could lift the curse of the dead.

sources.section: Third Age limitations and permanent death

paragraphs.text: Whether the magic that resists Zol differs from land to land or from realm to realm, the scholars do not agree. Nor is it known whether Zol finds a more fitting magic outside Aoaz.
Many traditions of magic are practised in Aoaz, and Varner is one practitioner among many. Bastian, a living human wizard and Varner’s contemporary, is famous throughout the Middle Lands.

The scholars distinguish four things in any great power: the power it holds, its ability to channel that power, its presence in a land, and its bodily shape. A being may have much of the first and little of the others, as Zol does.
paragraphs.note: The fourfold distinction is proposed; that Zol has immense power but no bodily form is established.

paragraphs.text: The people of Aoaz generally know the New Gods and the Old Gods, at least from their stories. Almost nobody holds the Holy Seven to be real beings of history, and He Who Was, Is and Will Be lies further still beyond common belief.

Mortals often take powerful Lesser Spirits for gods, and Great Spirits too can be worshipped. What people believe about a being’s rank is no sure proof of its true order. A town may raise a temple to a local Lesser Spirit in the belief that it is a New God.
paragraphs.note: The example of the town temple to a local Lesser Spirit is proposed.

sources.section: Gods are not equivalent to worshipped beings

paragraphs.text: The scholars hold that a being’s place in the order of being comes from its origin, not from the number of its worshippers. The much-feared Volgan is called a god by many, yet he remains a Great Spirit. Worship alone, they teach, cannot make a god.
paragraphs.note: The rule that origin and not worship decides rank, and that worship cannot make a god, is a working rule.

sources.section: Gods are not equivalent to worshipped beings

paragraphs.text: Whether any being can ever rise into the order of the gods, the scholars do not agree, and no teaching has settled the question.

The great example is the Deliverer. At the end of the Third Age many hailed him as the New God who saved Aoaz, and some saw miracles that none could deny. He was Afrit, and the true order of his being is not known. A great cult’s belief can be sincere and weighty in history without proving where a being came from.

plate.subject: black islands under a starless sky, no figure

paragraphs.text: Zol is the God of Death, an Old God, and the only Old God present in Aoaz. He came to Aoaz long before Aen and long before Volgan. His domain is the black north, Zol’s Mistake: a barren waste and all the black islands of the Kusmeel.

The Fading and the magic of Aoaz keep him from wielding his cosmic power freely, and he cannot keep an ordinary bodily form. Yet his power is immense, and servants of his are said to walk in the black north.

In the early ages Zol lay mostly dormant. When the Grand Alliance gathered in the First Age, his northern lands were already desolate, and they gave no armies and no aid to any side. Zol had no part in the Battle of Dardan. This was not weakness: under the Fading he could not cast his power freely abroad.

In the Second Age Elzon, the Great Necromancer, borrowed ancient magic linked to Zol to raise and bind the dead. It is the first stirring of Zol that the chronicles record. How Elzon came by that magic is not known, and no chronicle shows that Zol granted it or that the two were ever allied.

At the end of the Third Age Elzon drew too deeply on that old magic, and he died. Many scholars hold that Zol consumed him without ever stirring. Zol grew stronger, but he did not take the field, and he did not openly rule the war.
paragraphs.note: That Zol consumed Elzon is the favoured explanation, not established; Elzon’s death and Zol’s growing stronger without taking the field are established.

sources.section: Third Age limitations and permanent death

paragraphs.text: The Mistake is almost empty of the living and is roamed by the dead. Its seat is Furviatlon, and who keeps it for Zol is not known. No chronicle tells what mistake gave the land its name, or what the dead that wander it truly are.

Zol’s dead have risen beyond the Mistake. They are stronger than the corpses Elzon once raised, for the Old God’s own death-magic sustains them directly. Ordinary weapons cannot end them for good; only magic of great power can.
In the war of the north Zol took no body and did not come onto the field himself. His power went to war in other hands. Why Zol himself stayed away, no chronicle tells.
When the war of the north ended, Zol had not been slain. He had taken no body, and no blade of that war reached him. The black north remains his.
Zol has servants in Aoaz. He has no bodily form there and cannot take the continent by his own hand, and the scholars hold that what he does in Aoaz, he does through others.
His servants are not of one order. Spirits great and lesser are among them, so the oldest tales say.
What his servants do for Zol is not known. The scholars do not agree whether they bring him worship, souls, death, ritual, magic, sacrifice, relics or something else, or nothing at all.
It is not known whether his servants obey him willingly, under compulsion or for ends of their own. Who they are, no chronicle tells.

sources.section: Power is not the same as practical control

paragraphs.text: Nor is it known whether anything they do could ever give Zol a body in Aoaz.

plate.subject: green light filling a vast dark hall, no figure

paragraphs.text: Glernaen is the New God of Power and Wisdom, the mightiest of the twelve main New Gods of Aoaz. He answers the mortal need for strength and counsel, and the year begins with his month.
Glo, a crystal of old and holy power kept by Horos in the Castle of Yeldenne, is said to hold part of Glernaen’s power.

Like every god, Glernaen is never shown in the shape of a man. Of his own character and signs, his bonds with the other gods beyond his place as the mightiest of the twelve, how far he acts by his own will, and whether any cult of his own is kept in Aoaz, no chronicle tells. Nor is it known where Glo came from.
When the Man from the Ice lay beaten in the war, Glernaen and the New Gods restored him. Their joined power reached him through the crystal Glo.

plate.subject: storm and mountain shapes suggesting vast presences, no faces

paragraphs.text: Spirits have two ranks. The Great Spirits are the higher, immortal and capable of exceptional power; Volgan, Elzon and Horos are Great Spirits, and Elzon is also the Great Necromancer. The Lesser Spirits are the lower rank, also immortal, and some are still strong enough for mortals to take them for gods. Varner is a Lesser Spirit.

sources.section: Third Age limitations and permanent death

paragraphs.text: Great Spirits very rarely take the shape of men, and they are always beings of magic. Lesser spirits can be caught and used: the sorcerer-chief Gektor traps lesser spirits and bleeds them, though his claim to kill Great Spirits is only a boast.

Both ranks stand below the gods, yet rank is no chart of strength. Volgan, a Great Spirit, overcame a New God, and whether that god was one of the lesser New Gods is not known. The lesser New Gods are still stronger than most Great Spirits.

Great Spirits may rule domains, command followers or serve higher powers, but rule is no rank of its own. Volgan is a Great Spirit who became a sovereign and rules a realm; that names his place among the realms, not his kind.

Devils are corrupted Lesser Spirits, ancient and terrible; where they first came from, no chronicle of men tells. Devils are bound to their bodies and can be killed. A slain devil returns only through the lava rite, performed with its skull. Demons are another kind; the scholars of Selen hold them to be corrupted angels.
What divides a Great Spirit from a Lesser, how spirits came to be, how they stand toward angels and demons, and whether a spirit can change its rank, no chronicle tells.

Rank is not the only way to speak of a spirit. The scholars of Parim and Selen describe each spirit in three further ways: by its nature, by its origin and by its condition. These words overlap, and none of them adds a new order between the gods and the Great Folk.

By nature, the scholars speak of wild spirits of forest, mountain, beast and wilderness; veiled spirits of dreams, memory, hidden things and visions; elemental spirits of fire, wind, water, stone, ice and lightning; and the damned spirits of the very deep places under the earth.
paragraphs.note: The wild, veiled and elemental natures are proposed; the damned spirits of the deep are the accepted nature.

paragraphs.text: By origin, they speak of elder spirits, whose beginnings come before many peoples and realms; worldborn spirits, formed from the nature of places and forces such as forests, mountains, seas or storms; and godwrought spirits, made by an Old God or a New God for some purpose.

One spirit may bear several such names. Volgan is ancient beyond doubt, and the scholars call him an elder Great Spirit; whether he was worldborn or godwrought, and where he came from, no chronicle tells.
paragraphs.note: That Volgan is ancient is established; the descriptor elder Great Spirit is a working term.

paragraphs.text: By condition, a spirit may be embodied, holding a stable body; unbound, without a lasting body and free to move; bound to a place, an object or a person; dormant, existing but rarely able to act; or shattered, scattered in fragments after losing its unity.
These conditions belong to spirits and say nothing of the gods. An Old God without a body is not weak or idle for that, for the Old Gods are held by limits of their own.
paragraphs.note: The conditions are proposed; that the Old Gods have their own limits under the Fading is established.

plate.subject: a fissure under a mountain, cold lights far below

paragraphs.text: The damned spirits dwell in very deep places under the earth, far below the lands where folk live. They are also called blighted spirits, and the two names mean the same beings. The name blighted speaks of beings changed by curses, corruption or disaster, but it is not known whether every damned spirit was made so.
paragraphs.note: That corruption is the origin of every damned spirit is not confirmed.

paragraphs.text: In the First Age, in his great war, Volgan released damned spirits from very deep underground, and they marched in his army. Aoaz fell into disorder after that war, and some of these old threats may still linger in the deep places.

sources.section: First Age ethnic and political history

paragraphs.text: Much about them is not known: whether all of them are spirits in the strict sense, whether there are great and lesser among them, whether they were born in the deep world, driven there, imprisoned there or changed there, and whether they keep societies, ranks or lands of their own.
Nor is it known whether they have any bond with Volgan beyond that war, or with the dead of Zol’s Mistake, or how many of them have served him since.

entries.title: The Void
entries.subtitle: First Age · Place Beyond the World

paragraphs.text: The Void is the place beyond the world to which Volgan was banished after his defeat at the Battle of Dardan. He was banished, not destroyed.

In the Second Age the Great Necromancer Elzon, a Great Spirit and Volgan’s servant, freed his master from the Void after centuries of hard work. Volgan’s soul, or his spiritual presence, returned to Aoaz. The return was real, but the power stripped from him at Dardan did not come back with it, and he needed long years to recover.

The Void is not the Nether, the domain of the King of Demons in the south of the Ember Lands, and it is not the Abyss of the Ember Lands. No chronicle shows that the three are one place or that ordinary gates join them, and Elzon’s breach of the Void did not need to pass through either.
How Elzon reached into the Void, what it cost him, where his rite was done, and why the Great Spirits who had fought beside the Grand Alliance could not seal the prison again, no chronicle tells.
